sections.passage: A conversation between a customer and a technical support representative at a smart home technology company. The customer, Mrs. Patterson, calls because her newly installed smart thermostat is not functioning correctly. The support agent, James, asks for her account number and product model. Mrs. Patterson provides her account number HX-4492 and says she has the ThermoSmart Pro 3000 model, which she purchased three weeks ago. James pulls up her account and asks her to describe the problem. Mrs. Patterson explains that the thermostat screen keeps freezing and the temperature readings are inaccurate, sometimes showing temperatures that are five to eight degrees higher than the actual room temperature. James suggests several troubleshooting steps. First, he asks her to perform a soft reset by holding down the power button for ten seconds. Mrs. Patterson tries this but reports that the problem persists. Next, James recommends checking the Wi-Fi connection, explaining that the thermostat requires a stable 2.4 GHz connection to function properly and sync with the mobile application. Mrs. Patterson checks and confirms that her thermostat is connected to her 5 GHz network instead. James guides her through switching to the correct network frequency. He also mentions that there was a firmware update released last week, version 4.2.1, which specifically addresses temperature calibration issues. He walks her through downloading and installing the update, which takes approximately fifteen minutes. After the update completes, Mrs. Patterson reports that the temperature readings now appear accurate and the screen is responding normally. James schedules a follow-up call for the following Monday at 2 PM to ensure everything continues working correctly. He also reminds Mrs. Patterson that her product has a two-year warranty and she can contact support anytime during business hours, which are Monday through Friday, 8 AM to 6 PM.

sections.passage: A speech by the director of a community health centre introducing new wellness programmes available to local residents. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for attending this information session. My name is Dr. Sarah Mitchell, and I am the director of the Riverside Community Health Centre. I am delighted to announce several new wellness programmes that we are launching next month to support the health and wellbeing of our community. Our first new programme is called Mindful Mornings, a mental health initiative designed to help residents manage stress and anxiety. This programme will run every Tuesday and Thursday from 7 AM to 8:30 AM and will include guided meditation sessions, breathing exercises, and cognitive behavioural therapy techniques led by our licensed psychologist, Dr. Robert Chen. The programme is free of charge and open to all adults aged eighteen and over. Participants can register online through our website or by calling our reception desk at 020-7946-0321. Our second programme is the Active Aging Fitness Club, specifically designed for residents aged sixty and above. Sessions will take place on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays from 9 AM to 10:30 AM in our newly renovated gymnasium. The programme includes low-impact aerobics, strength training with resistance bands, balance exercises, and flexibility work. Our qualified physiotherapist, Emma Williams, will supervise all sessions to ensure safety and proper form. There is a nominal fee of five pounds per session, or residents can purchase a monthly pass for forty-five pounds, which represents a significant saving. We are also introducing a Nutrition and Cooking Workshop series, which will be held every Saturday from 10 AM to 1 PM. Our resident nutritionist, Dr. James Park, will teach participants how to prepare healthy, affordable meals. Each session will focus on a different dietary theme, such as heart-healthy cooking, managing diabetes through diet, plant-based nutrition, and meals for bone health. All ingredients will be provided, and participants will take home the meals they prepare. The cost is eight pounds per session. Finally, we are launching a Youth Sports Academy for children aged eight to sixteen. This programme will run during school holidays and will offer coaching in football, basketball, swimming, and tennis. All coaches are certified by the National Sports Association and have undergone background checks. The academy costs twenty-five pounds per week, and bursaries are available for families receiving government assistance. For more information about any of these programmes, please visit our website at www.riversidehealth.org or speak to our front desk staff after this session.

sections.passage: A discussion between two university students, Liam and Priya, and their professor, Dr. Anderson, about their research project on the impact of artificial intelligence on healthcare diagnostics. Liam begins by presenting their preliminary findings, which show that AI-powered diagnostic tools have demonstrated accuracy rates comparable to, and in some cases exceeding, those of experienced radiologists in detecting certain types of cancer from medical imaging. He cites a study from Stanford University where an AI system correctly identified skin cancer with an accuracy of 91 percent, compared to 87 percent for dermatologists. Dr. Anderson acknowledges the impressive statistics but cautions the students against presenting AI as a replacement for human doctors. She explains that the most effective approach is collaborative diagnosis, where AI serves as a screening tool that helps doctors prioritise cases and reduce diagnostic errors. She mentions that in the UK's National Health Service, AI tools are currently being used to screen for diabetic retinopathy, a condition that can lead to blindness if not detected early. Priya then raises the ethical concerns surrounding AI in healthcare. She discusses the issue of algorithmic bias, explaining that many AI diagnostic systems are trained primarily on data from Western populations, which may lead to less accurate results for patients from other ethnic backgrounds. She provides the example of dermatology AI tools that perform less accurately on darker skin tones because the training datasets contained predominantly lighter-skinned patients. Dr. Anderson praises this observation and suggests they include a section in their report on strategies for ensuring more diverse and representative training data. The discussion then moves to data privacy concerns. Liam points out that AI diagnostic systems require access to vast amounts of patient data, including medical records, imaging scans, and genetic information. He raises questions about who owns this data, how it is stored and protected, and whether patients should have the right to opt out of having their data used for AI training. Dr. Anderson references the General Data Protection Regulation, or GDPR, which provides a framework for data protection in Europe, but notes that regulations vary significantly across different countries. She encourages the students to compare regulatory approaches in at least three different regions for their report. The trio also discusses the potential for AI to improve healthcare access in underserved areas. Priya mentions a pilot programme in rural India where smartphone-based AI diagnostic tools are being used to screen for eye diseases in communities that have limited access to ophthalmologists. The programme has screened over 50,000 patients in its first year and has referred approximately 3,000 cases for further treatment. Dr. Anderson suggests this as a strong case study for their report. Finally, they agree on a timeline for completing their project, with a draft due in three weeks and the final submission in six weeks.

sections.passage: A university lecture on the sociological impact of social media on modern society. Good afternoon, everyone. Today's lecture examines how social media has fundamentally transformed the fabric of modern society, influencing everything from personal relationships and mental health to political discourse and cultural identity. Let us begin with the evolution of social media. The first recognisable social networking site, Six Degrees, was launched in 1997, allowing users to create profiles and list friends. This was followed by platforms like Friendster in 2002 and MySpace in 2003. However, it was the launch of Facebook in 2004 that truly revolutionised social networking. Originally limited to Harvard University students, Facebook expanded to the general public in 2006 and now has over three billion monthly active users worldwide. The subsequent emergence of Twitter in 2006, Instagram in 2010, and TikTok in 2016 further diversified the social media landscape. Now, let us consider the impact on interpersonal relationships. Social media has fundamentally altered how people form, maintain, and end relationships. On the positive side, it allows people to stay connected with friends and family across great distances, reconnect with old acquaintances, and form communities based on shared interests rather than geographical proximity. A 2023 survey by the Pew Research Centre found that 72 percent of adults use social media to stay in touch with friends and family, and 53 percent use it to meet new people with similar interests. However, the effects are not entirely positive. Research has shown that excessive social media use can lead to what psychologists call social comparison, where individuals constantly compare their lives to the curated, idealised versions presented by others online. A landmark study by the University of Pennsylvania in 2018 found that participants who limited their social media use to thirty minutes per day reported significant reductions in loneliness and depression over a three-week period compared to a control group. The impact on mental health, particularly among young people, is perhaps the most concerning aspect of social media's influence. Multiple studies have established correlations between heavy social media use and increased rates of anxiety, depression, body image issues, and sleep disturbances among adolescents. A 2022 report by the UK's Royal Society for Public Health found that Instagram was rated as the most negative social media platform for young people's mental health, particularly regarding body image and sleep quality. However, it is important to note that correlation does not imply causation, and some researchers argue that individuals with pre-existing mental health conditions may be more drawn to social media use. In the political sphere, social media has had a profound and complex impact. On one hand, it has democratised information sharing and given voice to marginalised communities. Social movements such as the Arab Spring in 2011, Black Lives Matter, and the climate change activism inspired by Greta Thunberg all leveraged social media to organise and amplify their messages. On the other hand, social media has also facilitated the spread of misinformation and disinformation, political polarisation, and foreign interference in democratic processes. A study by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that false news stories on Twitter spread six times faster than true stories, reaching significantly more people. The algorithms used by social media platforms, designed to maximise user engagement, often create what scholars call filter bubbles or echo chambers, where users are primarily exposed to information and viewpoints that reinforce their existing beliefs. This can lead to increased political polarisation and a fragmentation of shared reality. Economically, social media has created entirely new industries and transformed existing ones. The influencer marketing industry was valued at approximately 21 billion dollars in 2023, and social media platforms have become essential marketing channels for businesses of all sizes. The rise of social commerce, where consumers can purchase products directly through social media platforms, has blurred the lines between social networking and e-commerce. Looking to the future, emerging technologies such as virtual reality and augmented reality are likely to further integrate social media into daily life. The concept of the metaverse, a persistent virtual world where people can work, socialise, and play, represents the next frontier of social media development. However, this also raises significant questions about data privacy, digital addiction, and the potential for even deeper social isolation.

title.zh: 文章1 - 远程医疗的兴起

sections.passage: Telemedicine, the practice of delivering healthcare services remotely through telecommunications technology, has experienced remarkable growth over the past decade, accelerating dramatically during the COVID-19 pandemic. While the concept of remote medical consultation dates back to the early twentieth century, when doctors used radio and telephone to provide advice to patients in remote locations, modern telemedicine encompasses a far broader range of capabilities, including video consultations, remote patient monitoring, mobile health applications, and AI-assisted diagnosis. The origins of modern telemedicine can be traced to the 1960s, when NASA developed telemedicine systems to monitor the health of astronauts during space missions. These early systems transmitted physiological data from spacecraft to ground-based medical teams, enabling real-time health monitoring across vast distances. Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, telemedicine was primarily used to connect rural and underserved communities with specialist medical care in urban centres. However, the technology was expensive, unreliable, and limited in scope. The widespread adoption of the internet and mobile technology in the late 1990s and early 2000s transformed telemedicine from a niche capability into a viable healthcare delivery model. High-speed internet connections enabled real-time video consultations, while smartphones and wearable devices made continuous health monitoring practical and affordable. By 2019, the global telemedicine market was valued at approximately 50 billion dollars. The COVID-19 pandemic served as an unprecedented catalyst for telemedicine adoption. With lockdowns and social distancing measures making in-person medical visits difficult or impossible, healthcare providers around the world rapidly transitioned to remote consultations. In the United States, telehealth visits increased by 154 percent in the last week of March 2020 compared to the same period in 2019, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In the United Kingdom, the National Health Service reported that by April 2020, nearly 100 percent of GP consultations were being conducted remotely, compared to approximately 1 percent before the pandemic. The benefits of telemedicine are numerous. It improves access to healthcare for people in rural and remote areas, reduces travel time and costs for patients, minimises the risk of infectious disease transmission, and can help alleviate pressure on overburdened hospital systems. Studies have shown that telemedicine consultations for certain conditions, such as chronic disease management, dermatological assessments, and mental health counselling, can achieve outcomes comparable to in-person visits. For patients with mobility limitations, chronic conditions requiring frequent monitoring, or those living in areas with physician shortages, telemedicine can be transformative. However, telemedicine also faces significant challenges. The digital divide means that those who would benefit most from remote healthcare, including elderly populations and people in developing countries, often lack access to the necessary technology and internet connectivity. A 2022 study by the World Health Organisation found that approximately 2.9 billion people worldwide still lack access to the internet, severely limiting telemedicine's reach. There are also concerns about the quality of remote diagnoses, particularly for conditions that require physical examination, and about data privacy and security, as sensitive medical information is transmitted and stored digitally. Regulatory and reimbursement challenges further complicate telemedicine's implementation. Medical licensing laws in many countries restrict doctors from treating patients across state or national borders, and insurance reimbursement policies for telemedicine services vary widely. The lack of standardised protocols for remote consultations and the potential for overprescription of medication without thorough physical examination are additional concerns that healthcare systems must address.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Psychology of Consumer Decision-Making
title.zh: 文章2 - 消费者决策的心理学

sections.passage: Understanding why consumers make the purchasing decisions they do has been a central focus of marketing research for over a century. The field of consumer psychology explores the cognitive, emotional, and social factors that influence how people evaluate, select, and use products and services. While classical economic theory assumes that consumers are rational actors who make decisions based on a careful analysis of costs and benefits, decades of research in behavioural economics and psychology have revealed that human decision-making is far more complex, often driven by unconscious biases, emotional impulses, and social influences. One of the most influential frameworks for understanding consumer behaviour is the concept of heuristics, or mental shortcuts, identified by psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in the 1970s. Their groundbreaking work on prospect theory demonstrated that people tend to weigh potential losses more heavily than equivalent gains, a phenomenon known as loss aversion. In practical terms, this means that consumers are often more motivated by the fear of losing something than by the prospect of gaining something of equal value. Marketers frequently exploit this tendency through limited-time offers, countdown timers, and messages emphasising scarcity, such as 'only three items remaining in stock.' The anchoring effect is another powerful cognitive bias that influences consumer decisions. Research has shown that the first piece of information a consumer encounters, known as the anchor, disproportionately influences subsequent judgements. For example, if a product is initially displayed at a high price and then shown at a discounted price, consumers perceive the discount as a better deal, even if the final price is still higher than the product's actual market value. This explains why retailers often display the original price alongside the sale price and why negotiation typically begins with an artificially high starting point. Social proof, the tendency to follow the actions and opinions of others, is perhaps the most pervasive influence on consumer behaviour in the digital age. Online reviews, ratings, testimonials, and social media endorsements all serve as forms of social proof that can significantly impact purchasing decisions. A 2023 survey by BrightLocal found that 98 percent of consumers read online reviews before making a purchase, and 84 percent trust online reviews as much as personal recommendations from friends or family. Businesses recognise this and actively cultivate positive reviews, respond to negative ones, and partner with influencers to leverage their credibility and reach. The role of emotions in consumer decision-making cannot be overstated. Neuroscientific research has shown that emotions play a critical role in the decision-making process, often preceding and guiding rational analysis. Antonio Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis suggests that emotional responses to past experiences create physiological signals that influence future decisions. In marketing, this translates to the importance of brand storytelling, emotional advertising, and creating positive associations between products and desirable feelings such as happiness, belonging, security, or aspiration. Apple's marketing strategy, for example, has long emphasised creativity, innovation, and individuality rather than simply listing technical specifications. The digital revolution has fundamentally transformed the consumer decision-making process. The traditional linear model of awareness, interest, desire, and action has evolved into a complex, non-linear journey involving multiple touchpoints across online and offline channels. Consumers now research products extensively before purchasing, with the average consumer consulting eleven pieces of content before making a buying decision, according to Google's consumer journey research. The rise of comparison shopping, price-tracking tools, and personalised recommendations powered by artificial intelligence has given consumers unprecedented access to information and options, potentially leading to more informed decisions but also contributing to decision fatigue and choice overload. Cultural and socioeconomic factors also play significant roles in shaping consumer behaviour. Cross-cultural research has revealed substantial differences in purchasing patterns, brand preferences, and decision-making styles across different cultures. For instance, consumers in collectivist cultures, such as Japan and China, tend to place greater emphasis on brand reputation and social conformity, while consumers in individualist cultures, such as the United States and Australia, may prioritise personal expression and uniqueness.

title.en: Passage 3 - Urbanisation and the Future of Cities
title.zh: 文章3 - 城市化与城市的未来

sections.passage: For the first time in human history, more than half of the world's population lives in urban areas. According to the United Nations, 56 percent of the global population, approximately 4.4 billion people, resided in cities in 2022, and this proportion is projected to increase to 68 percent by 2050. This unprecedented urbanisation presents both enormous opportunities and formidable challenges for governments, planners, and citizens alike. The history of urbanisation is closely tied to industrialisation. Before the Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain in the late eighteenth century, the vast majority of people lived in rural areas and worked in agriculture. The shift to factory-based manufacturing drew millions of people to cities in search of employment, leading to rapid and often unplanned urban growth. By 1900, London had become the world's largest city with a population of 6.5 million, a figure that would have been unimaginable just a century earlier. The twentieth century saw urbanisation accelerate dramatically, particularly in developing countries. Cities like Tokyo, Mumbai, São Paulo, and Lagos grew at extraordinary rates, often outpacing the development of infrastructure and public services. Today, Tokyo remains the world's largest metropolitan area with approximately 37 million inhabitants, followed by Delhi with 32 million and Shanghai with 29 million. The challenges of rapid urbanisation are well documented. Housing shortages are among the most pressing issues, as the demand for affordable accommodation consistently outstrips supply. In many developing cities, this has led to the proliferation of informal settlements or slums, where residents live in substandard conditions without adequate access to clean water, sanitation, or electricity. The UN estimates that approximately one billion people currently live in slums, a number that is expected to increase significantly in the coming decades. Urban sprawl, the uncontrolled expansion of urban areas into surrounding countryside, presents environmental and social challenges. Sprawling cities require more extensive transportation networks, leading to increased car dependency, longer commute times, and higher carbon emissions. A study by the University of Toronto found that residents of sprawling cities in the United States drive an average of 40 percent more kilometres per year than residents of compact, densely built cities. In response to these challenges, urban planners and policymakers have developed various strategies for creating more sustainable, liveable cities. The concept of the 'smart city' has gained significant traction in recent years, leveraging technology and data to improve urban services, reduce waste, and enhance quality of life. Singapore, often cited as the world's smartest city, uses an extensive network of sensors and cameras to monitor traffic flow, air quality, waste management, and energy consumption in real time. The city-state's Smart Nation initiative has led to innovations such as autonomous vehicle testing, digital government services accessible through a single smartphone application, and predictive analytics for urban maintenance. Copenhagen has emerged as a global leader in sustainable urban planning. The Danish capital aims to become the world's first carbon-neutral capital by 2025, having already reduced its carbon emissions by 42 percent since 2005. Key initiatives include an extensive cycling network used by 62 percent of residents for their daily commute, a district heating system powered largely by renewable energy, and innovative waste-to-energy plants that convert household waste into electricity and heat. The city's Nordhavn district serves as a model for sustainable urban development, featuring energy-efficient buildings, car-free zones, and integrated green spaces. Barcelona's 'superblocks' initiative represents another innovative approach to urban redesign. The programme reorganises city blocks to prioritise pedestrians, cyclists, and green spaces over car traffic. Within superblocks, through traffic is redirected to perimeter roads, freeing up interior streets for community gardens, playgrounds, outdoor dining, and cultural activities. Early results from the programme show reductions in air pollution, noise levels, and traffic accidents, alongside increases in local business activity and community engagement. Green infrastructure, including urban forests, green roofs, and permeable surfaces, is increasingly recognised as essential for sustainable cities. Urban trees provide shade, reduce the heat island effect, absorb air pollution, and support biodiversity. Singapore's commitment to becoming a 'city in a garden' has resulted in over 300 kilometres of park connectors and the integration of vegetation into building facades and rooftops throughout the city. Similarly, Melbourne's ambitious plan to plant 3,000 trees per year aims to increase canopy cover and combat rising temperatures exacerbated by climate change.

prompt.en:
The diagram below shows the process of recycling plastic bottles, from collection to the manufacture of new products.

Stage 1: Used plastic bottles are collected from recycling bins, households, and commercial establishments.
Stage 2: The collected bottles are transported to a sorting facility where they are separated by plastic type (PET, HDPE, PVC) using infrared scanning technology.
Stage 3: Sorted bottles are compressed into bales and sent to a washing facility where labels, caps, and adhesive residues are removed.
Stage 4: Clean bottles are shredded into small flakes approximately 5mm in size.
Stage 5: The flakes are further sorted by colour using optical sensors and then undergo a hot washing process to remove any remaining contaminants.
Stage 6: Dried flakes are melted at temperatures exceeding 260 degrees Celsius and extruded into small pellets called nurdles.
Stage 7: Nurdles are sold to manufacturers who use them to produce new products such as clothing fibres, packaging materials, automotive parts, and new bottles.

Summarise the process by selecting and reporting the main stages. Write at least 150 words.
prompt.zh:
下面的流程图展示了塑料瓶回收的过程，从收集到新产品的制造。

阶段1：使用过的塑料瓶从回收箱、家庭和商业机构收集。
阶段2：收集的瓶子被运输到分拣设施，使用红外扫描技术按塑料类型（PET、HDPE、PVC）进行分离。
阶段3：分拣后的瓶子被压缩成捆，送往清洗设施，在那里去除标签、瓶盖和粘合剂残留物。
阶段4：干净的瓶子被粉碎成约5毫米大小的小碎片。
阶段5：碎片通过光学传感器进一步按颜色分类，然后经过热水清洗过程以去除任何剩余污染物。
阶段6：干燥的碎片在超过260摄氏度的温度下熔化，挤出成称为nurdles的小颗粒。
阶段7：Nurdles被出售给制造商，用于生产新产品，如服装纤维、包装材料、汽车零部件和新瓶子。

通过选择和报告主要阶段来总结流程。至少写150个单词。

prompt.en:
Some people argue that technological advancement is the key to solving the world's most pressing problems, such as climate change, disease, and poverty. Others believe that technology creates more problems than it solves and that society should focus on simpler, more traditional approaches.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

一些人认为技术进步是解决世界上最紧迫问题（如气候变化、疾病和贫困）的关键。另一些人则认为技术带来的问题比它解决的更多，社会应该专注于更简单、更传统的方法。

讨论两种观点并给出你自己的意见。
